probe.format_note: 9:16 vertical, 2742 frames, 15.3 MB. Stereo HE-AAC 44.1 kHz at 59 kb/s. Two-second mean RMS measured, not listened to: quiet start at 0-2 s (-24.8 dB), then a loud, dense mix between about -14.6 and -22.5 dB with no real rest; loudest at 12 s (-14.7), 32 s (-14.7) and 44 s (-14.6); the windows at -20 dB or lower start at 4 s (-20.6), 34 and 36 s (-21.4, -20.7), 52 s (-20.0), 62 s (-20.4) and 70 s (-22.5, during the closing lockup).

rights_note: found by the owner on Pinterest with a style search (file «kinetic typography.mp4»), given by the owner via Downloads/refrencee on 2026-11-03; origin not stated → plan mode ADAPT, never RECREATE

mode.alt_film_mode: UI when the content package shows software, an app or a workflow
mode.why: third-party film of unknown origin: borrow the motion language and look only, never its shots one by one, its logos, its product names, its copy, its UI screens or its person (owner note); a voiceover package defaults to REEL, and the reference's strongest material is word-by-word kinetic type

ignored.why: the fixed caption 'New Claude opus 5.5' with its emoji is third-party copy and a product name; only the idea of one small line that stays still above the moving screen is reusable

the laptop itself, its keyboard, menu bar and app dock with real app icons, the room wall and the hand in the first half second are the reference's own props; they are never copied as they are (see risks for the screen-in-a-dim-room device)

all the English copy is third-party and is never reused: the swear-word lines ('NO FUCKING WAY', 'ARE YOU FUCKING KIDDING ME?!', 'FUUUU'), 'OKAY', 'CAN YOU BELIEVE', 'I DID NOT TOUCH AFTER EFFECTS', 'THIS ISN'T AN MCP', 'MADE WITH ONE PROMPT' and the rest; the brand voice never takes the swearing, only its rhythm

the 'Higgsfield' name and squiggle logo, the 'KATANA' wordmark with its flame ornaments, the 'Claude' and 'Claude Motion' marks, the 'After Effects' name and the 'MCP' diagram labels are third-party branding

third-party UI and data: the chat app screens, the connector steps, the account 'creator@higgsfield.ai', the address 'https://mcp.higgsfield.ai/mcp', the permission page and the catalog images with faces and figures are never reused; a how-to for another company's product is not our content
the real person, their mask, jacket, hands and room are never copied, nor the offer lines ('Comment KATANA', '3 Day free trial', 'new users') and the lime UI plate above them

method: ffprobe; ffmpeg contact sheets fps=2 at 480 px (16 sheets, all viewed); scene detect gt(scene,0.3) found only 72.60, 84.23, 85.70, 85.80, 88.40 and 89.03 s, because 0-72.6 s is one continuous filmed shot of a screen and the screen fills only about a third of the frame; so nearly every row boundary before 72.6 s is placed by eye from the 2 fps sheets, accurate to about 0.25 s. Sheet frames were read as nominal time plus 0.25 s, the offset of the fps filter, checked against the cuts at 72.6 and 84.23 s. Dense 15 fps sheets over 1.3-2.9, 9.2-10.8, 47.2-48.8, 71.9-73.5 and 83.8-85.4 s; boundaries inside those windows are accurate to about 0.07 s. Two-second mean RMS of the audio with astats. Colours were read by eye, not sampled. The audio was measured, not heard, so voice versus music is not separated and beat sync was not tested.

visual_language: Word-by-word kinetic typography, in which almost every spoken word is its own hit, played on a screen that is itself being filmed in a dim room. The film has three parts: 0-72.6 s the type film on the filmed laptop, 72.6-84.23 s a plain full-frame phone walkthrough with word captions, and 84.23-91.5 s a personal close with a call to action. Type: very heavy extended and condensed all-caps grotesques in big sizes, usually filling the width of the screen, with occasional contrast from a hair-thin weight, a mono face in the prompt box, outline letters, and one serif italic line; words stack into posters across several beats. Rhythm: 60 screen beats in 72.6 s, an average of about 1.2 s, while a new word arrives about every 0.3-0.7 s inside a beat; the main holds are the logo lockups (about 1.5 and 2.6 s) and the poster moments; there is one deliberately slow beat before a slash (42-43.5 s) and one black breath (47.9-48.0 s). Moves come in very fast from heavy directional blur and settle in 2-4 frames with a sharp ease-out, then keep creeping slowly. Sound-sync was not tested. Palette: three alternating fields, black with red bloom, pure red, off-white, flipping on almost every word, with black and white type and one red dot as a recurring full stop; a chapter turns fully grey as a contrast; one acid yellow word appears once; the third part is near-black with lime. Signature moments: a word that bursts from a point of light; the red X that cuts a window apart; a word that grows up and down from a laser line; the burst shape that inverts letters; the big stretch of one word; a whole poster losing weight and falling off the screen; a dial with a sentence that announces the slash, then delivers it.
look: Two layers. Inner layer, the screen content: flat type planes with 2.5D moves, occasional extruded letters, tilted perspective planes, a dot-grid floor, one real 3D cube; light comes only from glows: strong red bloom and halation around the type, laser lines with flares, drifting bokeh dots, sparks. Depth of field is an effect: blurred word states, a giant out-of-focus word as a backdrop, heavy motion blur and echo copies on every whip. Materials: matte black, glass cards with a thin bright border, plain paper white, pure flat red. Outer layer, 0-72.6 s: real photographic depth: one phone camera shot of a laptop lid, its dark keyboard falling away to black at the bottom, and a warm tan wall lit from behind the lid. The physical light reacts: the exposure pumps against the screen, so on white or red frames the wall goes dark brown and the keyboard nearly disappears, and on dark frames the wall lifts to pale cream and the backlit keys appear. The screen occupies the full width and about a third of the height, and shows halation and slight softness. The part after 72.6 s has no outer layer. The final part is warm, realistic live footage.
code_translation: Everything inside the screen is code-native and fits HTML/CSS/SVG in headless Chromium: word stacks as DOM, directional and zoom blur by frame blending or scaled copies, echo trails as stacked copies, slashes by clip-path and SVG strokes, masks at a laser line, shape morphs in SVG, inversion with mix-blend-mode, bloom with blurred copies, dot grid and bokeh on canvas. The cube and any object that is 3D in the reference stay real 3D in three.js, with perspective planes for the tilted type, never flattened. The outer layer, if L4 keeps it, is also built in code as real depth: render the screen film first, then map it onto a laptop or other device lid in three.js with a dim room, or as a perspective plane, and drive the wall and keyboard brightness from the mean luminance of the screen on each frame, inverted, to reproduce the exposure pump; add a little handheld drift. A real filmed look cannot be matched fully, but no footage is needed. About 92% of the running time can be built without footage, counting that wrapper; the 7.3 s with the real person (84.23-91.5 s, about 8%) cannot and L4 replaces them with a scene from our voice-over in this film's rendering, never a fake real person.
continuity: One filmed frame holds the whole type film together: the device, the wall and one fixed caption line stay still while everything inside the screen changes.
The world around the screen reacts: wall and keys pump against the brightness of each frame, so the outer shot feels alive with no cut.
A full stop as an actor: the round accent dot stays with the words, then swells into a full-frame wipe.
The laser line as a horizon: words are born from it, it runs under a name, it shrinks to a single beat, and comes back as the closing lockup, so the same mark opens many scenes.
Words carry across colour flips: the same word stays in place while its field jumps from red to black, so the change reads as a hit, not a cut.
An exit leaves a trail: stacked echo copies of the old frame are the road into the new one; whips and zooms pass through repeats of what was just on screen.
A glow survives a whip: a red glow leaves one layout and locks into the next object.
A slash is the universal scene-changer: a thin stroke cuts on a diagonal, the frame splits along it and the next field shows under it.
A big field shrinks into the next object (a white page becomes a card), and an object is entered by zooming through its button.
The poster builds up: words appear alone first, then stand together, so the viewer reads the sentence twice.
Text stays, object changes, and the other way round: a headline scrambles while its window stays still, or a window is destroyed under a headline that stays.
Recap by pile: earlier words return as a tower that recedes in depth, and the next word lands over its ghost.

Tension through contrast: a slow small sentence announces the next hit; then all energy dies by weight loss and a page falling off the screen, then one black breath before a new chapter in a new colour.
A slot-reel vertical roll swaps a question with the answer; the two share one centre line.
A list where only the current step is filled and the rest stay in outline shows progress without any arrow.
risks: Third-party film of unknown origin: ADAPT only. Never copy the logos, product names, English copy, UI screens, account, address, catalog images, laptop, dock icons, room or person, or the shot order one by one.

The laptop in a dim room belongs to the reference's footage, and the router says props and setting come from the voice-over. Its presentation idea (the film played on a lit screen in a dark room, with the room reacting) is a real part of the look and may be kept as a framing device only if it suits the voice-over; L4 decides and records it. The film must still work if the type fills the whole 9:16 frame.

On the filmed laptop the screen is only about a third of the frame height, with the middle band for type and large dead areas in the wall and keyboard. Persian lines at the reference's size may fall below readable sizes on a phone: readability ranks above the reference, so enlarge the device or crop into it, and keep text within the safe zone (the caption at about 17% of the height and the keyboard area carry no meaning).

The pace is extreme: a new word about every 0.3-0.7 s and a new screen about every 1.2 s, for more than a minute. Persian hold times and minimum sizes win over this pace; our cuts follow the voice timing, and the fast pace is kept by moves, not by shorter holds on words the viewer must read.

Most of the type tricks are built on separate Latin capitals: letters that land loose, per-letter resolve, tracking and stretching, one repeated letter, a letter holding an eye. Persian letters must stay correctly joined: apply them to whole words or to masks over shaped text, use a kashida for stretching, and follow references/rtl-grammar.md, which also reverses sweeps, typing, pans and the line journey to run right to left. Persian has no capitals, so heavy weights do that work.

The look relies on very heavy display weights and on hair-thin to black weight changes. These depend on the brand's fonts: if the brand font has no such range or no variable axis, use the heaviest and lightest cuts available with a cross-fade, and never swap to a non-brand font.

Colours were read by eye. Red, black, off-white, the single yellow word and the lime in the last part map onto brand colour roles (main field, dark surface, light surface, accent); never used as literal values, and a brand's banned colours win. If the brand has no strong hot colour, the whole energy of the film shifts, and L4 must pick the strongest allowed accent for the field and bloom.

Fast full-field colour flips between white, red and black on nearly every word are a flicker risk for sensitive viewers, and they compress poorly; keep them in brand roles and do not go faster than the voice requires.
The swearing and the angry tone are part of the source's voice. They never enter the film; the shout-like moves must come from our voice-over's own emphasis, or be softened to fit the owner's tone.
The middle section (72.6-84.23 s) is a plain how-to with a different look from the rest; it is reusable only if the content package has real steps, and then as DOM UI of our own.

The reference has its own loud audio, which was measured, not heard, and beat sync was not tested. Our film's cuts follow the voiceover first, and L6 places accents on our cuts rather than reusing its sound.
